extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, artists, and social reformers
extracted.subtask_short: critique of poetry and social realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for assessing lyrical poetry, prose style, travel-writing, satire, and the truthful artistic representation of the people (peasantry) in literature and visual art. Emphasises concreteness, direct observation, fidelity of depiction, and stylistic qualities like melody, simplicity, and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric brevity and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric poetry is at its best in short pieces—'short swallow flights of song'—that feel like songs and suggest a twin melody; brevity and rippling music are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and wording: poems should read as if each must have 'a twin melody' born in the same moment; the finest products are short lyrics that combine simplicity and musical feeling. Avoid overextended lyric production; mercurial temperament and concise form suit lyric power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple pathos and pregnant simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: A greatest poetic power lies in simple pathos and 'pregnant simplicity'—the natural, concentrated expression of tender emotions that can indicate a whole history in a single quatrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative examples: Heine's manner likened to Wordsworth's 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways' and Tennyson's 'Circumstance.' Aim for pure feeling 'breathed in pure music,' avoiding unnecessary images or thoughts that dilute the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional range and deft transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A lyric should display a wide compass of notes—sombre sublimity, dreaminess, sorrow, shuddering horror, idyl, overflowing fun—and be able to move quickly between laughter and tears without seeming artificial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective transitions (even from the lofty to the ludicrous) require poetic sensibility to 'poise our emotion and expectation' so sudden falls have impact. Use changes of tone sparingly and with craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagistic economy and imaginative expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling may be represented by a brief image (a finely cut cameo), expanded into mysterious dreams, or dramatized as little stories (half ballad, half idyl); images should convey feeling without artificiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for images that develop 'by the same beautiful necessity' as natural forms; avoid forced ornament or contrivance. The image should be precise and suggest wider feeling or story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional elevation to symbolic or sublime thought
rubrics_metrics.description: While grounded in song and feeling, a poet should sometimes soar to higher regions—using picturesque symbolism, flashing sublime thought, and pouring forth loftier strains of hope or indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elevation should be rare and earned (example: the closing stanzas of Heine's 'Deutschland' invoking Dante-like fury). Avoid making lofty symbolism the constant mode of lyric voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose clarity, rhythm, and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good prose should be crystalline, definite, clear, compact, and rhythmically varied; avoid labyrinthine sentences, long chains of adjectives, and parenthetical digressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heine's prose is praised as 'allotropic' German—'compact, metallic, brilliant'—showing delicate precision, felicities of word and cadence. Strive for varied rhythm, epigrammatic pith, imaginative grace, and economical sentences rather than clumsy, heavy constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit and satire: subtlety and allusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and wit should be subtly prepared, slyly allusive, and finely edged rather than broad and blunt; the power of satire often increases with age and craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heine's sarcasms are 'subtly prepared and so slily allusive' that they can 'escape readers whose sense of wit is not very acute.' Prepare satirical strokes with context and irony rather than mere invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and balance in travel-writing and mixed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel-literature ('Reisebilder') and hybrid forms should run the gamut of moods—from droll and fantastic to sombre and terrible—and balance humor with poetic sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor in these forms should be 'aërial and sprite-like,' not persistent; juxtapose modes (humor, poetic feeling, tragedy) to show breadth but avoid tonal incoherence. Use striking transitions (as in the hospital example) to create effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness of associated imagery as test of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The range and fixity of concrete images associated with a collective term ('railways', 'the people') indicate how much concrete knowledge the speaker has of the thing in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who conjures many distinct, role-based images (navvy, engineer, traveller, director, landed proprietor) demonstrates fuller experiential knowledge than one who only thinks of a 'Bradshaw' or a single station. Use varied, concrete image-sets to show expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct observation over inherited tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists and writers should base representations on direct observation and sympathy with the subject rather than on idyllic literature or inherited prepossessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of painters and novelists who rely on tradition leading to false portrayals (opera peasants, idyllic ploughmen). Encourages artists to study actual peasants, speech, and habits rather than copying literary conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity in representing the people’s true motives and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing the working-classes, depict the motives and influences that actually act upon them, not the motives that moralists think ought to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsification is especially pernicious in portrayals of the people because art's power to extend sympathy can be misdirected. Present the 'peasant in all his coarse apathy' and the 'artisan in all his suspicious selfishness' honestly to ground reform and sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological as well as external truth in social novels
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist's gift for external idiom and gesture must be matched by truthful rendering of psychological character and inner life; external accuracy alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against authors who copy colloquial style accurately but lapse into 'preternaturally virtuous poor children' or melodramatic psychology. Strive to move from humorous/external traits into emotional and tragic truth without losing realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical study and specific facts for social reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Social and political understanding requires thorough study—recording habits, maxims, class interactions, influence of local conditions, and effects of religious doctrines—presented with specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages occupation-holders (landholder, clergyman, mill-owner) to register observations so a coherent natural history of social classes can inform reformers; praises Riehl as a model. Books 'well nourished with specific facts' are most useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local color: physical types, dialects, proverbs, and songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate depiction of peasantry and provincial groups requires attention to enduring physical types, dialects, phraseology, proverbs, and songs which persist as 'provincial style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: regional physiognomies (Hessian type), baptismal name persistence, Wendish customs. Use specific, localized detail (customs, names, animal treatment) to give topographical authenticity and historical continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate model selection for historical or regional truth
rubrics_metrics.description: To depict historic or regional characters truthfully (e.g., medieval types), artists should seek living models among peasantry who preserve older physical and cultural types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that 'a painter who wants to draw mediæval characters with historic truth must seek his models among the peasantry.' Use authentic models rather than modern, cultivated types when historic fidelity is required.
